difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring a reverse-causation resolution: patients receiving the more aggressive treatment have worse outcomes, yet the treatment itself is effective. Test-takers must recognize that severity of illness, not treatment, drives the correlation.
stimulus: At a large urban hospital, patients who received an aggressive antibiotic regimen for bacterial pneumonia had a 30-percent higher in-hospital mortality rate than patients who received a standard regimen. Yet clinical trials conducted under controlled conditions consistently show that the aggressive regimen is more effective at eliminating the bacteria responsible for the pneumonia.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The aggressive antibiotic regimen is significantly more expensive than the standard regimen and is therefore used less frequently overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Physicians at the hospital prescribed the aggressive regimen primarily to patients whose pneumonia was already at an advanced or critical stage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several of the antibiotics used in the aggressive regimen have known side effects that can worsen certain pre-existing heart conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The clinical trials that evaluated the aggressive regimen were conducted at teaching hospitals with above-average staffing ratios.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacterial pneumonia accounts for a smaller proportion of pneumonia cases at urban hospitals than at rural ones.

explanations.correct: If the aggressive regimen was reserved for the most critically ill patients, those patients were already more likely to die regardless of treatment. The higher mortality rate reflects patient severity, not treatment failure — dissolving the conflict between hospital outcomes and clinical-trial results.
explanations.A: Cost and frequency of use explain how often the regimen is prescribed but not why those who receive it have worse outcomes. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. Identifies a confounding variable — pre-treatment severity — that accounts for both the worse hospital outcomes and the genuine clinical efficacy of the aggressive regimen.
explanations.C: Side effects on heart conditions could partially worsen outcomes, but this explains only some deaths and only in a subpopulation; it doesn't reconcile the broad discrepancy with consistently superior clinical-trial results.
explanations.D: The conditions under which the trials were conducted might affect trial generalizability, but this deepens the paradox by suggesting the hospital context is less optimal — it doesn't explain why aggressive-regimen patients die at higher rates.
explanations.E: The urban/rural distribution of pneumonia types is irrelevant to the discrepancy between hospital outcomes and clinical-trial efficacy within the same institution.

difficultyReason: Economic policy paradox with a self-selection / composition-effect resolution. Test-takers must identify that the businesses surveyed after the minimum-wage increase are a biased sample — only survivors remain — making aggregate wage data appear favorable despite the policy's costs.
stimulus: Following a significant increase in the regional minimum wage, a survey of businesses in the region found that the average hourly wage paid to employees had risen by less than the amount of the minimum-wage increase. Yet economists confirm that every business in the region is complying fully with the new minimum wage law.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The minimum wage increase was phased in gradually over an 18-month period rather than taking effect all at once.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many businesses in the region responded to the minimum wage increase by reducing the total number of hours worked by their employees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A substantial number of businesses that had employed large numbers of minimum-wage workers closed permanently before the survey was conducted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The survey methodology relied on self-reported payroll data, which some economists consider less reliable than tax-record data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the years before the minimum-wage increase, average wages in the region had been rising steadily at approximately two percent per year.

explanations.correct: If businesses that heavily employed minimum-wage workers shut down before the survey, the surviving businesses — which had fewer minimum-wage employees to begin with — would show a smaller average wage increase even while fully complying with the new law. This survival-bias effect reconciles full compliance with a below-expected average wage rise.
explanations.A: A phase-in period might slow the full impact, but full compliance is confirmed, so the average wage should still reflect the full new minimum among current employees. This resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Reducing hours affects total compensation but not the hourly wage rate. A lower hourly average is still unexpected if all firms comply with the minimum; this doesn't explain why the average hourly wage rose less than the minimum-wage increase.
explanations.C: Correct. A classic survivor/selection-bias resolution: the post-increase business sample is biased toward firms with fewer minimum-wage workers, producing a lower measured average increase despite universal compliance.
explanations.D: Potential measurement unreliability would cast doubt on the survey results generally, but it doesn't explain the specific directional discrepancy — it equally might cause overestimates. This is an irrelevant-methodology distractor.
explanations.E: Pre-increase wage trends are irrelevant to why, after a confirmed compliance, the measured average increase falls short of the statutory increase.

difficultyReason: Environmental policy paradox with a temporal/scope-difference resolution. Test-takers must identify that aggregate pollution figures conceal a compositional shift: the reduction in one source is offset by a growth in another, explaining why national totals are unchanged despite the regulated sector's compliance.
stimulus: After regulations requiring a 40-percent reduction in sulfur dioxide emissions from coal-fired power plants took effect, the power industry achieved exactly the required reduction. Nonetheless, total sulfur dioxide emissions measured across the nation remained unchanged from pre-regulation levels.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sulfur dioxide is one of several pollutants regulated under the same environmental statute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The monitoring equipment used to measure national sulfur dioxide levels was upgraded in the same year the regulations took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several environmental advocacy groups had lobbied for a 60-percent reduction rather than the 40-percent reduction that was enacted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During the period when the regulations were being implemented, the number of diesel-powered industrial vehicles operating nationwide increased sharply, substantially raising sulfur dioxide output from that sector.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Power plants that burn natural gas emit far less sulfur dioxide per unit of energy produced than do coal-fired plants.

explanations.correct: A compensating increase in sulfur dioxide from a different, unregulated source — diesel vehicles — would offset the power industry's verified reduction, leaving national totals flat. This confounding variable reconciles both halves of the apparent contradiction.
explanations.A: The existence of other regulated pollutants doesn't address why sulfur dioxide specifically remained unchanged. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Upgraded monitoring equipment could affect what is detected, but if anything more sensitive equipment would record lower totals after a genuine reduction. This doesn't explain unchanged national totals and potentially deepens the paradox.
explanations.C: Whether 60 percent would have been preferable is entirely irrelevant to why a confirmed 40-percent reduction failed to lower national totals. Irrelevant.
explanations.D: Correct. Identifies a confounding variable — a contemporaneous increase in emissions from an unregulated sector — that fully accounts for unchanged national totals despite genuine compliance by the regulated sector.
explanations.E: Natural gas versus coal emission rates might be relevant to policy choices, but the stimulus concerns coal-plant compliance and national totals; this fact doesn't explain why verified power-plant reductions were offset at the national level.

difficultyReason: Technology-domain paradox requiring recognition of a definitional / measurement-scope distinction. Test-takers must see that 'customer satisfaction' and 'customer retention' measure different populations at different points in the product lifecycle, creating an apparent but not genuine contradiction.
stimulus: A software company introduced an extensively redesigned version of its flagship product. Surveys conducted three months after the launch showed that customer satisfaction scores for the new version were significantly higher than scores for the previous version. Yet the company's overall customer retention rate dropped noticeably in the same three-month period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The satisfaction surveys were completed only by customers who had already chosen to continue using the product after the redesign.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company increased the subscription price of the product at the same time it released the redesigned version.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Software products typically receive higher satisfaction scores immediately after a major redesign than they do after several months of use.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some longtime customers reported that they preferred the visual layout of the previous version of the product.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The company's customer support staff received additional training in the months preceding the product launch.

explanations.correct: If only customers who stayed with the product filled out the satisfaction survey, those respondents are a self-selected group — precisely the customers who liked the redesign enough to keep using it. Customers who were dissatisfied and left would not appear in the survey. This selection effect explains why satisfaction scores are high (only happy stayers were surveyed) while retention dropped (many customers left without being counted in the satisfaction data).
explanations.A: Correct. Classic self-selection / survivorship bias: the high satisfaction scores reflect only the retained, satisfied subset, not the full customer base, reconciling high measured satisfaction with lower overall retention.
explanations.B: A price increase could cause customers to leave, explaining lower retention, but it would not explain why satisfaction scores among remaining customers are higher than before. This resolves one horn only (retention drop) while deepening the other (why would satisfaction rise if the price went up?).
explanations.C: A honeymoon effect on satisfaction scores would predict scores drop over time, but it doesn't reconcile simultaneously high satisfaction scores with simultaneously low retention in the same three-month window. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: A subset of longtime customers preferring the old layout could contribute to departures, but 'some' customers is too vague to account for a noticeable retention drop, and it does nothing to explain why satisfaction scores rose. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Better customer support training would tend to improve both satisfaction and retention, if anything deepening the paradox of why retention fell while satisfaction rose.
